source.title: Why do Larger Models Generalize Better? A Theoretical Perspective via the XOR Problem

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether increasing width can improve test performance among zero-training-error solutions, using a three-layer convolutional network on XORD rather than the one-hidden-layer networks named in V2.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own width-dependent XORD test-error results and MNIST width/initialization comparisons. The clustering and initialization analyses are not results about any listed version's measured property, so they are summarized under fits_no_version. Values in the relevant plots are not stated in text and remain figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study tests V2's width–generalization relationship using XORD convolutional networks, including comparisons restricted to zero-training-error solutions, and provides theoretical guarantees comparing small and overparameterized networks. It is not an original source of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors prove, under assumptions in a simplified XORD setting, that exploration at initialization and weight clustering can yield better-generalizing global minima in larger networks. MNIST experiments demonstrate related clustering and feature-transfer effects.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a three-layer convolutional network with max pooling and a fixed fully connected layer on synthetic XORD data, plus MNIST experiments; it does not reproduce the one-hidden-layer width study described in V2.
record.method_sensitivity: The XORD experiment varies channel count and reports results both over all runs and over zero-training-error runs. The MNIST comparison varies training set size and initialization; cluster initialization changes the training procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained MNIST filters have smaller angles to four cluster centers than randomly initialized filters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training can concentrate convolutional filters around a few prototypes.

fits_no_version.finding: A four-channel MNIST network initialized from a trained 120-channel network's cluster centers improves and nearly matches the larger network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transferring clustered filters from a larger network can improve a smaller network's test performance.

fits_no_version.finding: On the classic XOR task, wider networks optimize successfully more often, but all four possible inputs are training examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Greater width improves optimization through exploration at initialization.

record.problems: The principal XORD width results are shown in figures without exact values in the text. The XORD task is synthetic and has limited expressive complexity; the authors explicitly note the network VC dimension is at most 15. MNIST test-error values are also presented as plots without text-stated numbers.
record.rows_left_out: None. Figure 1 rows preserve each reported width and distinguish all-run averages from the zero-training-error subset. Figure 4b results are included as figure-only comparisons; its exact training-set-size-specific values are not stated in text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.

The original one-hidden-layer MNIST/downsampled-CIFAR-10 setting; a controlled fixed-recipe width sweep trained to convergence; and the interpolation-threshold peak associated with double descent. MNIST comparisons do not establish that both widths interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizer generalization and tuning breadth.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted large-batch recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with other measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: The direct decoy-set comparison: k=2 and k=100 both reach zero training error, but only the larger network recovers the XORD function. Appendix D supplies another such comparison with a non-diverse negative training point.

Theoretical comparison on diverse training sets: for k≥120, target recovery has probability at least 1−c−16e^−8 under the stated assumptions; for k=2, convergence to a global minimum failing to recover the target has probability at least (1−c)33/48. These are guarantees, not empirical frequencies.

Sample-complexity separation among zero-training-error solutions: when p+=p−=0.98, δ≤0.05 and ε<0.005, the large-network bound is at most 2 samples versus at least 129 for the small network; a second example gives 2 versus 17. For p+,p−≤0.7 the bound provides no separation, which is not evidence that the effect is absent.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's MNIST limits_scope verdict: successful compression through transferred initialization does not show that widening fails. Individual figure-only states remain cannot_determine, while the explicit textual width trend supports the grouped XORD verdict. The channel sweep also changes learning rate inversely with width, and exact plotted errors are unavailable.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train on random labels or compare natural-label and random-label held-out performance.

The study uses a three-layer convolutional network on XORD and MNIST, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; it does not test the interpolation-threshold peak or double descent.
No fully connected versus convolutional comparison is reported.
The paper does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD or test tuning breadth.
The paper does not compare batch sizes or measure a large-batch generalization penalty.
The paper does not test dropout or its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
The paper measures weight clustering but not magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with the training-test gap.
The paper does not remove memorized training examples or measure the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: MNIST convolutional network (4 channels)

rows.check: This measures transfer of learned cluster centers and restricted retraining, not widening beyond interpolation. Its improvement cannot justify a limits_scope verdict on V2.
